newsitem.title: FRANCE: New Saudi grain import to test EU resolve.
newsitem.headline: New Saudi grain import to test EU resolve.

text.p: Saudi Arabia has started a scramble to sell it barley in a major new import tender, but its biggest recent supplier, the European Union, may not be getting a big share of the action this time round, grain traders said.
Saudi Arabia, the world's top barley importer, surprised the grain market on Friday with a tender to buy 700,000 tonnes, with a tight deadline of July 15 for the barley to reach its ports.
Grain firms had been lying in wait for a new import tender following a purchase of 500,000 tonnes in April. But most had expected deliveries to be stretched out over a longer period.
Friday's announcement will trigger a race against the clock to sell the barley and start loading vessels in June, a month when the EU has rules in force to discourage sales.
"It's too risky. There's too little time to turn round and cover the merchandise," one European grain exporter said.

"Everything depends on the willingness of Brussels as far as (export) subsidies are concerned," he said, adding that the European Commission seemed happy to rein in exports for now after sales rose substantially in the past year.

Its fiercest current competitor is Canada, estimated to have one to two million tonnes of exportable barley in its stocks. Australia and the United States, two other major exporters, have rather tighter available supplies for now, traders said.
Saudi Arabia dominates world barley trade with imports of around five million tonnes a year to feed its animal herds.

By placing the deadline earlier than expected, Riyadh has put European exporters and the Commission on the spot, since the schedule does not leave time to wait for the next harvest in a couple of months' time. Supplies at several ports are tight.
Subsidised European export barley is currently around $150 per tonne, having gained $8 to $10 over the past two months.
Traders must send Riyadh their offers to supply the barley on May 19, three days before the next weekly opportunity to secure EU export subsidies and gauge EU export policy on May 22.
Most would normally run the risk of selling before knowing how far the EU intends to help them match lower world prices with subsidy. But this time the EU has left them little rope.
Current EU rules mean 20 Ecus ($23) per tonne would have to be taken off any subsidy awarded if the ship is loaded in June.

That would wipe out the latest available subsidies of 15.90 Ecus ($18) per tonne and leave the exporter out of pocket. The alternative would be to gamble on extra quantities being granted by Brussels immediately or hope the EU would ease the loading penalty for June -- both uncertain in the current tight market.
At its most recent weekly export subsidy auction on Thursday this week, the EU granted aid for 89,200 tonnes of exports, seen covering short-term requirements at a price of $150-151 a tonne.
Latest EU figures show it has sold just over six million tonnes of barley from last year's harvest, compared with just 1.6 million tonnes at the same point in the previous season.

While it is not as worried about restraining barley exports as those for wheat -- subjected to a rare export tax for the second time in a year to knock domestic prices -- EU officials have hinted they are satisfied to see barley exports stop soon.
